records.title: Coolant Hose and Thermostat Housing Leaks
records.description: The Probe's cooling system uses multiple small coolant hoses and a plastic thermostat housing that become brittle with age. Leaks develop at hose connections and the thermostat housing cracks, leading to overheating that can damage the aluminum cylinder heads.
records.solution: Replace all coolant hoses and the thermostat housing. Upgrade to an aluminum thermostat housing if available. Replace the thermostat itself and flush the cooling system with fresh coolant.

communityRecommendations.content: Replace ALL coolant hoses at once when one fails — if one is brittle enough to leak, the others are close behind

records.title: Cooling-system neglect leads to overheating and head-gasket failure on the KL V6
records.description: On the 2.5L KL-DE V6, an aging cooling system is the main path to serious engine damage. Original thermostats (mounted under the intake/coolant pipe housing) stick, water pumps weep, radiators clog, and the system loses pressure, allowing the engine to overheat. Repeated overheating warps the aluminum heads or breaches a head gasket, after which owners report coolant loss, bubbles in the reservoir with the cap on, and continued overheating even after a thermostat swap. The tightly packaged V6 makes cooling maintenance easy to defer, which is precisely what leads to the expensive failure.
records.solution: Refresh the cooling system proactively: thermostat, radiator cap, water pump, hoses, and radiator as needed, and bleed air properly since the V6 is prone to air-lock. Diagnose a suspected head gasket with a combustion-gas (block) test or by watching for bubbles in the coolant. Confirmed head-gasket failure requires head removal, resurfacing check, and new gaskets. Address overheating immediately to avoid warping the heads.
symptoms: Temperature gauge climbing into the red
Coolant loss with no obvious external leak
White exhaust smoke or sweet smell

records.title: Distributor Internal Coil and Sensor Failure
records.description: The Probe's Mazda-sourced 2.0L and 2.5L V6 engines use a distributor with integrated ignition coil and cam/crank sensors. The internal components overheat and fail, causing intermittent stalling and no-start conditions. The 2.5L V6 KL engine version is particularly prone.
records.solution: Replace the distributor assembly. Remanufactured units are available. Ensure the O-ring seal is replaced to prevent oil leaks. Check the ignition wires and spark plugs at the same time.
symptoms: Engine cuts out at operating temperature
Stalls when hot and restarts when cool

records.title: Distributor internal oil seal failure contaminates crank/cam sensor, causing stalling and no-start
records.description: The Probe's cam-driven distributor (Mazda-sourced, shared with the 626/MX-6) has an internal shaft oil seal that hardens with age and lets engine oil migrate into the distributor housing. The oil fouls the optical crank-angle/cam sensor and the internal igniter electronics, producing erratic trigger signals. This is one of the most frequently reported drivability failures on these cars, especially early 1993-1994 units, with documented onset as low as ~70,000 miles. Because the distributor also carries the ignition pickup, a failed seal eventually kills spark timing entirely. Ford also addressed related intermittent-stall complaints on this platform through the internal igniter/coil.
records.solution: Replace the distributor with a good reman or known-good used unit, and always pull the cap on any replacement to reject any that show oil inside (a sign the seal has already failed). Some rebuild the optical sensor and reseal the shaft. Correcting any upstream oil leak (cam seal/valve cover) that raises housing oil level helps. On a running-but-rough car, cleaning the optical disc and connector can be a temporary measure. Re-set base timing with a light after installation.

records.title: GF4A-EL / 4EAT automatic transmission slips, shifts harshly, and develops seal leaks
records.description: The Mazda-derived electronically controlled 4-speed automatic (GF4A-EL / 4EAT-G, with seven valve-body solenoids) is the weak point on automatic-equipped Probes. A thin aluminum thrust washer in the torque converter sheds particles that abrade the bushings, Teflon sealing rings, and rubber seals, causing internal leaks and loss of line pressure with age. The transmission then slips, hunts between 2nd and 3rd, shifts hard from 1st to 2nd, or occasionally falls out of gear when passing. Once slipping from worn seals begins, a partial fix rarely holds and a full rebuild is usually required.
records.solution: Start with a fluid and filter service and verify correct fluid level, and inspect for external leaks and a failing solenoid/valve-body pack, which can cause similar symptoms cheaply. A Transgo shift kit can correct some harsh 1-2/2-3 shift complaints without removal but does not cure worn-seal slippage. Confirmed internal slippage calls for a complete rebuild or a reman unit. Manual-swap conversions are a known enthusiast path given the shared Mazda drivetrain. Keep the transmission cooler and fluid fresh to prolong life.
symptoms: Jumps out of gear when accelerating

records.title: Pop-up (retractable) headlight motors seize or fail from corrosion and worn gears
records.description: Both second-generation Probe engines use concealed pop-up headlights driven by electric retractor motors, one per side. Water intrudes into the motor connectors and gearset, corroding contacts and stripping the plastic drive gears, so one or both lights fail to rise, stick partway, or drop unexpectedly. It is a signature age-related failure of these cars and a nighttime safety concern when a light won't open. Remanufactured motors are commonly sold with stronger redesigned gears, confirming this was a recognized OEM weakness.
records.solution: Diagnose which side has failed by manually cycling the headlights and checking the retractor relay and fuses. Clean corroded connectors and pack them with dielectric grease; lubricate the pivot linkage. If the motor gears are stripped or the motor is seized, replace the retractor motor assembly (used and reman units are readily available from the shared Mazda parts pool). Preventively grease connectors and pivots to extend motor life.
symptoms: Headlight stuck up, down, or partway open
One light works, one does not
Grinding or clicking from headlight bucket

records.title: Power Window Motor Burnout
records.description: The power window motors burn out prematurely, particularly on the driver's side. The Mazda-sourced motors are undersized for the heavy glass. The window may work intermittently before failing completely.
records.solution: Replace the window motor. The regulator usually survives and can be reused. Lubricate the window tracks with white lithium grease to reduce motor strain.
symptoms: Motor clicks but window doesn't move

fixParts.note: Motor only for the front left/driver window on 1993-1997 Ford Probe. Reuse the regulator if serviceable and confirm side before ordering.

records.title: Timing Belt Failure on 2.5L V6
records.description: The 2.5L KL-DE V6 engine is an interference design, meaning a broken timing belt causes catastrophic valve and piston damage. The belt should be replaced every 60,000 miles but many owners miss this interval.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, and idler pulleys at 60,000-mile intervals. Replace the water pump at the same time since it is driven by the timing belt. Budget for a complete timing belt kit.

records.title: Timing belt failure destroys the 2.0L I4 (interference engine)
records.description: The 2.0L FS four-cylinder DOHC is an interference design: if the timing belt snaps or jumps, the pistons strike open valves and bend them, requiring head work. Ford specifies belt replacement at 60,000-mile intervals, but many surviving cars are decades past that and running on original or long-forgotten belts. (The 2.5L KL V6 is generally regarded as non-interference, so a V6 belt failure typically leaves the car stranded but without valve damage, which makes the risk asymmetric between the two engines.) Owners frequently overlook the interval because the car still runs fine right up until the belt lets go.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt every 60k miles (or sooner given age-hardened rubber), and do the water pump, tensioner, idler, and cam/crank seals at the same time since they share access. On a 2.0L that has already jumped or snapped the belt, plan for a cylinder-head removal to replace bent valves, or an engine swap. Keep documentation of the last belt service given the cars' age.
symptoms: Sudden loss of power / engine dies while driving
Rattling or slapping from front timing cover
